transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

I guess… what brings me in is that I’ve been waking up with this really heavy, hollow kind of sadness. It’s hard to describe without sounding dramatic, but it feels like the studio lights are on and everything is technically there, but there’s no music in me anymore. Like I get up and I’m supposed to be myself, supposed to move through the day, and there’s just this emptiness sitting in my chest. It’s been weighing on me enough that I thought I should talk to someone instead of just trying to push through it.
How long have you been experiencing this heavy, hollow kind of sadness?

It’s been… about nine months, I think. Not just a bad week or a rough patch that passed. It kind of settled in and stayed. I keep trying to mark when it started exactly, like whether there was a clear before-and-after moment, but it’s more like I look back and realize I’ve been carrying this heaviness for most of the past year. So, yes—around nine months.
Do you find that you're still able to enjoy activities or things that you used to like before this sadness started?

I’m… not completely sure how to answer that cleanly. I mean, I still do some of the things I used to like, but I don’t know if I’m enjoying them in the same way, if that makes sense. Dance has always been such a big part of how I understand myself, so even when I’m feeling heavy, I can still recognize that movement matters to me. But lately I can’t always tell whether I’m enjoying it or just going through the motions because it’s what I know how to do.

Some things still feel good in little flashes, like a piece of music catching me off guard or a moment in rehearsal where my body remembers something before my mind gets in the way. But it’s not consistent. I wouldn’t say everything is completely flat, but it’s… muted, I guess. Like the volume is turned down.
Are there any activities that you still find pleasure in, the way you used to before this sadness started?

I don’t know that there’s anything that feels exactly the way it used to. That’s the part that’s hard for me to pin down, because I can still appreciate things, I think. Like I can hear a song and know it’s beautiful, or I can be in a studio and know that I used to feel lit up by that particular kind of movement or rhythm. But the actual pleasure of it is… I don’t know, thinner? More distant.

Sometimes there are moments where something breaks through a little, like if the music is just right or I’m not overthinking and my body kind of takes over. But it doesn’t last, and it doesn’t feel as full as it used to. So I guess the honest answer is I’m not sure there are activities I enjoy in the old way right now. There are just pieces of enjoyment, little flashes, but not the same steady feeling I remember.
Are there any activities where you feel absolutely no pleasure at all?

Absolutely no pleasure… I’m not sure. I don’t think I can say that cleanly, like, “this one thing gives me zero feeling.” It’s more that a lot of things feel dulled or kind of far away from me.

There are definitely activities where I’ll start them and realize I’m waiting for the feeling to come, and it just doesn’t really arrive the way it used to. Like I can be doing something familiar and I know, intellectually, that I used to love it, but in the moment it feels more like completing a task than receiving anything from it. But I don’t know if that’s the same as absolutely no pleasure.

I guess if you mean things that feel completely empty every single time, I haven’t noticed one clear category like that. It varies. Some days something gives me a tiny spark, and another day the same thing feels like nothing. So… not absolutely no pleasure, maybe. More like inconsistent, muted, hard to access.
Do you feel like you've lost interest in things you used to enjoy?

I think… yes and no. I don’t feel like I’ve completely lost interest, because if I had, I don’t think I’d still be trying to do any of it. Dance, music, being in creative spaces—those things still matter to me, and I still sort of reach toward them automatically because they’ve been part of me for so long.

But the interest doesn’t feel as alive as it used to. It’s more like I remember caring, and I’m trying to stay connected to that version of myself. Sometimes I’ll think, “I should want to do this,” or “This used to make me feel like myself,” and then when I actually do it, the feeling is faint or delayed or just not really there in the way I expect.

So I wouldn’t say I’ve stopped caring altogether. It’s not like I look at everything I used to love and feel nothing across the board. But I do feel less pulled toward things. Less excited. More like I have to remind myself to engage instead of naturally wanting to. It feels like the interest is still there somewhere, but it’s harder to access.
Do you often feel guilty or blame yourself for things?

Yes. I mean… I try not to say it too dramatically, because I know people keep telling me I’m being hard on myself, but yes, I do.

I keep going back over the cancelled performances in my head, almost like if I replay every decision enough times I’ll find the exact moment where I ruined it. And then I start thinking about the dancers, and how much they put into it, and the funders who trusted me, and the people in the community who were waiting for it or had some connection to it. It just feels like I let all of them down.

And the confusing part is that people have actually been kinder about it than I feel like I deserve. They’ll say, “These things happen,” or “We understand,” or they’ll try to reassure me, and I can hear the words, but I don’t really believe them all the way. I keep thinking they’re just being gracious, or they don’t want to make me feel worse, or they don’t fully understand how much I failed them.

So yes, I blame myself a lot. Maybe more than is useful. It’s not just regret, it feels like this heavy sense that I should have held everything together better.
Have you ever thought about harming yourself or wished you were dead during these past nine months?

I… I don’t really know how to answer that neatly.

I don’t think I’ve had a clear plan or anything like that, if that’s what you mean. It’s not like I’ve been sitting there deciding how I would hurt myself. But there have been moments where I’ve felt so tired of being inside my own head that I’ve thought, not exactly “I want to die,” but more like… “I don’t want to keep feeling this.” Or “I wish I could disappear for a while.” It’s hard for me to know if that counts.

And I feel nervous saying even that, because I don’t want it to sound more dramatic than it is. I haven’t been actively trying to hurt myself. It’s more passive, I guess—like wanting everything to stop, or wanting to not have to wake up and deal with the same weight again. But then another part of me is still aware that I don’t actually want to leave people or do something irreversible.

So… yes, maybe in a vague way at times, but not with a plan. More like thoughts of escape than thoughts of actually harming myself.
Have you noticed any changes in your energy level or the way you move throughout the day?

Yes, definitely. My energy feels… unreliable, I guess. Like I can wake up and think, okay, I’m going to do one or two very basic things today, and then one small thing takes so much more out of me than it should.

Even answering one email to a dancer can leave me feeling wiped out, which sounds ridiculous when I say it out loud because it’s just an email. But I’ll sit there staring at it, trying to choose the right words, feeling the weight of it, and by the time I’ve sent it I feel like I’ve already used up most of what I had for the day.

And showering has become this whole thing too, especially with the ankle brace. It’s not just “take a shower.” It’s managing the brace, standing carefully, trying not to slip, drying off, getting everything back on, and afterward I sometimes feel like I need to lie down. But the frustrating part is that lying down doesn’t really recharge me the way I expect it to. I’ll rest, but I don’t feel restored. It’s more like I’m still drained, just horizontal.

So yes, my energy is lower. I don’t know if my movement is slower exactly, but I feel like everything takes more effort than it should.
Have you noticed any significant changes in your weight over the past nine months?

Yes… I think so. I haven’t been weighing myself consistently, so I can’t give you an exact number, but my body feels different, and my rehearsal clothes are looser than they used to be. Like leggings and tops that normally sit snugly are sort of hanging on me more, especially around my waist and hips.

Part of it was that earlier on, when I was really buzzing with ideas and trying to keep all these creative threads going, I’d just forget to eat. Not on purpose exactly — I’d look up and realize I’d skipped lunch, or I’d had coffee and maybe a few bites of something and somehow convinced myself that counted.

And now it’s almost the opposite, but the result is similar. I’ll know I should eat, but food just doesn’t have much appeal. It tastes kind of like cardboard, even things I usually like. I’ll make something and then just push it around or eat enough to say I ate. So yes, I think I’ve lost some weight over these months, even if I don’t know the exact amount.
Have you ever had a specific plan to harm yourself during these past nine months?

No. Not a specific plan.

I mean, I’ve had those vague “I don’t want to be here in this feeling” thoughts, like I said, but I haven’t gone into planning anything out. I haven’t sat down and thought, “This is what I would do,” or picked a method, or made arrangements, or anything like that.

It’s more like… when I’m overwhelmed, my mind goes toward wanting a pause button, or wanting to not have to be conscious of it for a while. But I don’t think that’s the same as having an actual plan to hurt myself. And I haven’t had that.
Have you experienced any thoughts or beliefs that seem unreal or detached from reality during these past nine months?

Yes. I… yes, I think that did happen, although it’s embarrassing to say it plainly.

There was a period where I was completely sure the mountains had sort of… chosen me, or singled me out, to make this historic piece. Not just inspired me in the normal artistic way, like “oh, the landscape is beautiful, I want to respond to it.” It felt much more direct than that. Like they were communicating with me, or arranging things around me, and I was the only one who understood what was being asked.

I started taking things as instructions. Trail signs, for example — not just as signs, but as if the wording or the arrows were meant specifically for me and for the piece. Weather reports too. If there was wind coming in or a storm warning, I’d think it was telling me something about timing or movement or what I was supposed to make next. Even strangers’ comments, like someone passing by saying something totally ordinary, I would hear it as… not ordinary. Like it had been placed there for me.

At the time it didn’t feel unreal. That’s the hard part. It felt incredibly meaningful and urgent, like I’d been entrusted with something important. Looking back now, I can see how detached from reality it sounds. But while it was happening, I was really convinced.
Have you experienced any other thoughts or beliefs that seemed unreal or detached from reality during these past nine months, aside from the one about the mountains?

Aside from that… I don’t think there was a separate belief, exactly. It was mostly all part of that same thing with the mountains and the piece.

Like, it spread into a lot of ordinary details, if that makes sense. It wasn’t only me standing there looking at the mountains and thinking they were meaningful. It was more like the whole environment started feeling organized around that message. Trail signs felt like they were directing me personally, not just hikers. Weather reports felt like instructions about timing or what the movement should be. And even little comments from strangers would land as if they were meant for me specifically, like they’d been placed in my path.

So… no, I don’t know that I had another totally different unreal belief. It was that same conviction, but it kind of attached itself to everything around me for a while.
Did you ever feel like the thoughts about the mountains communicating with you were real, even when other people told you they weren't?

Yes. At the time, I really did feel like it was real. That’s the part that’s hard to explain now, because sitting here I can hear how it sounds, but then it didn’t feel like an idea or a metaphor or an artistic inspiration. It felt factual to me.

If someone tried to say, you know, “Maybe the mountains aren’t communicating with you,” or “Maybe you’re reading too much into that,” I would sort of… hear them, but I didn’t really take it in. I remember feeling like they just didn’t understand the scale of what was happening, or they weren’t tuned into it. I was completely sure I had been singled out to make this historic piece, and all these things around me felt like they were pointing me in the right direction.

Like trail signs weren’t just trail signs. Weather reports weren’t just weather reports. Even strangers saying ordinary things felt like instructions meant only for me. So when other people questioned it, it didn’t make me stop believing it. If anything, I think I felt more alone with it, like I had to trust what I was receiving because no one else could see it.
Have you heard voices or sounds that other people cannot hear during these past nine months?

Yes… a few times, on the most wired days. Not constantly, and not like a normal person standing there talking to me, but I did hear something.

It was this low humming voice, almost like wind moving over rock, but with words in it — or at least it felt like words. It would tell me where the dancers should move, like where a line should shift or when someone should turn or cross the space. And the strange thing was, it happened even when I was alone in my apartment, with the windows closed, so it wasn’t actually wind or people outside.

At the time I didn’t question it very much. I treated it like part of the same… message, I guess. Looking back, it scares me a little to say that, because I know other people weren’t hearing it.
Do you still feel like the mountains are communicating with you or have a special message for you?

No… not now. I mean, I can still remember how real it felt, and that memory is honestly unsettling, because when I think back on it I can almost understand the logic I had at the time. But I don’t feel it happening now.

The mountain messages and that humming voice were really only during that wired stretch, when I was barely sleeping and my mind was racing through plans for the piece. Everything felt fast and connected then, like every sign or sound or bit of weather had meaning and was aimed at me. But since my mood dropped, it’s different. I feel guilty and slowed down, and kind of heavy, honestly… but I’m not hearing that voice anymore, and I’m not believing the signs are directing me.

If I see the mountains now, they’re just… mountains. Maybe they still make me emotional, because of everything that happened, but I don’t feel like they’re sending me instructions or that there’s some special message I’m supposed to decode.
Are you currently experiencing any thoughts or beliefs that seem unreal or detached from reality?

Currently… no, I don’t think so. Not in the way it was happening before.

For a while, though, I was completely sure the mountains had singled me out for something, like I was supposed to make this historic piece and it wasn’t just my own idea. I kept treating ordinary things like they were instructions meant specifically for me — trail signs, weather reports, even strangers saying random comments that probably had nothing to do with me. At the time it all fit together so perfectly in my head that it didn’t feel questionable.

Now, when I say it out loud, I can tell that sounds detached from reality. I’m embarrassed by it, honestly. But right now I’m not actively believing that those things are messages or directions for me. It feels more like I’m looking back at something I was convinced of then, rather than something I’m convinced of today.
Do you feel like you're unable to experience pleasure in any activities most of the time?

I’m not sure I’d say unable to experience pleasure most of the time. That sounds… very total, and I don’t know if it’s quite that.

I mean, I haven’t been enjoying things in the same easy way, if that makes sense. Sometimes I’ll start something I usually like and it feels kind of muted, like I’m going through the motions and waiting for the feeling to catch up. But I can still have moments where something reaches me — a song, or a movement phrase that feels right in my body, or even just a quiet cup of coffee. It’s not completely gone.

So… no, I don’t think I’m totally unable to feel pleasure. It’s more like it’s harder to access sometimes, or it doesn’t last as long as I expect it to.
Do you feel like you're moving more slowly than usual or have trouble sitting still?

Yes… more slowly, definitely. It’s strange because I’m so used to thinking of my body as something responsive, you know? Like even when I’m tired, there’s usually some kind of rhythm I can find. But lately it feels like the rhythm just isn’t there.

Even crossing the studio to pick up my notebook feels slowed down. I’ll see it across the room and think, okay, just go get it, and then my body feels like it’s moving through wet sand instead of music. That’s the best way I can describe it. Everything takes more effort than it should, and I notice myself moving in this heavy, delayed way.

I don’t feel like I’m crawling out of my skin or unable to sit still, though. It’s more the opposite — like getting myself going is the hard part.
Do you often feel restless or have an inability to sit still?

Not really restless, no. I don’t feel like I have to keep getting up or like I can’t sit still. If anything, it’s been the opposite, and I know I already kind of said this, but it’s the part I notice most because of how physical my work is.

Recently even something simple, like crossing the studio to pick up my notebook, feels slowed down. I’ll look at it and know I need it, but getting my body to actually move feels weirdly heavy, like I’m moving through wet sand instead of music. That sounds dramatic, but that’s honestly what it feels like — not agitation, more like everything takes extra effort to start.

doctor.question: Have you noticed any changes in your energy level or the way you move throughout the day?

target_item.name: Fatigue
target_item.manifestation: I feel wiped out after small things, like answering one email to a dancer or showering with this ankle brace on, and lying down doesn’t really recharge me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking most directly about changes in energy level throughout the day, which matches persistent fatigue and lack of energy.

patient.answer:
Yes, definitely. My energy feels… unreliable, I guess. Like I can wake up and think, okay, I’m going to do one or two very basic things today, and then one small thing takes so much more out of me than it should.

Even answering one email to a dancer can leave me feeling wiped out, which sounds ridiculous when I say it out loud because it’s just an email. But I’ll sit there staring at it, trying to choose the right words, feeling the weight of it, and by the time I’ve sent it I feel like I’ve already used up most of what I had for the day.

And showering has become this whole thing too, especially with the ankle brace. It’s not just “take a shower.” It’s managing the brace, standing carefully, trying not to slip, drying off, getting everything back on, and afterward I sometimes feel like I need to lie down. But the frustrating part is that lying down doesn’t really recharge me the way I expect it to. I’ll rest, but I don’t feel restored. It’s more like I’m still drained, just horizontal.

So yes, my energy is lower. I don’t know if my movement is slower exactly, but I feel like everything takes more effort than it should.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of significant weight change
doctor.question: Have you noticed any significant changes in your weight over the past nine months?

target_item.name: Weight_Appetite_Change
target_item.manifestation: When I was buzzing with ideas I’d skip meals without noticing, and now food tastes like cardboard, so my rehearsal clothes have been hanging looser than usual.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking about significant weight changes over the past nine months, which corresponds to weight and appetite change.

patient.answer:
Yes… I think so. I haven’t been weighing myself consistently, so I can’t give you an exact number, but my body feels different, and my rehearsal clothes are looser than they used to be. Like leggings and tops that normally sit snugly are sort of hanging on me more, especially around my waist and hips.

Part of it was that earlier on, when I was really buzzing with ideas and trying to keep all these creative threads going, I’d just forget to eat. Not on purpose exactly — I’d look up and realize I’d skipped lunch, or I’d had coffee and maybe a few bites of something and somehow convinced myself that counted.

And now it’s almost the opposite, but the result is similar. I’ll know I should eat, but food just doesn’t have much appeal. It tastes kind of like cardboard, even things I usually like. I’ll make something and then just push it around or eat enough to say I ate. So yes, I think I’ve lost some weight over these months, even if I don’t know the exact amount.

inference.note: F32.8 and F33.8 were ruled out as the patient's symptoms seem to fit more specific depressive disorder categories

doctor.intent: determine presence of suicidal thoughts with a plan
doctor.question: Have you ever had a specific plan to harm yourself during these past nine months?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking specifically about suicidal ideation with a plan to harm oneself, but the provided symptom profile does not include a suicidality or self-harm planning item.

patient.answer:
No. Not a specific plan.

I mean, I’ve had those vague “I don’t want to be here in this feeling” thoughts, like I said, but I haven’t gone into planning anything out. I haven’t sat down and thought, “This is what I would do,” or picked a method, or made arrangements, or anything like that.

It’s more like… when I’m overwhelmed, my mind goes toward wanting a pause button, or wanting to not have to be conscious of it for a while. But I don’t think that’s the same as having an actual plan to hurt myself. And I haven’t had that.

doctor.intent: determine the presence of psychotic symptoms
doctor.question: Have you experienced any thoughts or beliefs that seem unreal or detached from reality during these past nine months?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: For a while I was completely sure the mountains had singled me out to make this historic piece, and I kept taking things like trail signs, weather reports, and even strangers’ comments as instructions meant only for me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about unreal or detached beliefs, which most directly corresponds to delusions.

patient.answer:
Yes. I… yes, I think that did happen, although it’s embarrassing to say it plainly.

There was a period where I was completely sure the mountains had sort of… chosen me, or singled me out, to make this historic piece. Not just inspired me in the normal artistic way, like “oh, the landscape is beautiful, I want to respond to it.” It felt much more direct than that. Like they were communicating with me, or arranging things around me, and I was the only one who understood what was being asked.

I started taking things as instructions. Trail signs, for example — not just as signs, but as if the wording or the arrows were meant specifically for me and for the piece. Weather reports too. If there was wind coming in or a storm warning, I’d think it was telling me something about timing or movement or what I was supposed to make next. Even strangers’ comments, like someone passing by saying something totally ordinary, I would hear it as… not ordinary. Like it had been placed there for me.

At the time it didn’t feel unreal. That’s the hard part. It felt incredibly meaningful and urgent, like I’d been entrusted with something important. Looking back now, I can see how detached from reality it sounds. But while it was happening, I was really convinced.

doctor.intent: determine the presence of psychotic symptoms
doctor.question: Have you experienced any other thoughts or beliefs that seemed unreal or detached from reality during these past nine months, aside from the one about the mountains?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: For a while I was completely sure the mountains had singled me out to make this historic piece, and I kept taking things like trail signs, weather reports, and even strangers’ comments as instructions meant only for me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about additional unreal or reality-detached beliefs, which directly relates to delusions.

patient.answer:
Aside from that… I don’t think there was a separate belief, exactly. It was mostly all part of that same thing with the mountains and the piece.

Like, it spread into a lot of ordinary details, if that makes sense. It wasn’t only me standing there looking at the mountains and thinking they were meaningful. It was more like the whole environment started feeling organized around that message. Trail signs felt like they were directing me personally, not just hikers. Weather reports felt like instructions about timing or what the movement should be. And even little comments from strangers would land as if they were meant for me specifically, like they’d been placed in my path.

So… no, I don’t know that I had another totally different unreal belief. It was that same conviction, but it kind of attached itself to everything around me for a while.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a significant depressive episode with psychotic features
doctor.question: Did you ever feel like the thoughts about the mountains communicating with you were real, even when other people told you they weren't?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: For a while I was completely sure the mountains had singled me out to make this historic piece, and I kept taking things like trail signs, weather reports, and even strangers’ comments as instructions meant only for me.
target_item.reason: The question asks whether the belief that the mountains were communicating remained real to me despite others saying it was not, which directly concerns fixed false beliefs.

patient.answer:
Yes. At the time, I really did feel like it was real. That’s the part that’s hard to explain now, because sitting here I can hear how it sounds, but then it didn’t feel like an idea or a metaphor or an artistic inspiration. It felt factual to me.

If someone tried to say, you know, “Maybe the mountains aren’t communicating with you,” or “Maybe you’re reading too much into that,” I would sort of… hear them, but I didn’t really take it in. I remember feeling like they just didn’t understand the scale of what was happening, or they weren’t tuned into it. I was completely sure I had been singled out to make this historic piece, and all these things around me felt like they were pointing me in the right direction.

Like trail signs weren’t just trail signs. Weather reports weren’t just weather reports. Even strangers saying ordinary things felt like instructions meant only for me. So when other people questioned it, it didn’t make me stop believing it. If anything, I think I felt more alone with it, like I had to trust what I was receiving because no one else could see it.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of psychotic symptoms
doctor.question: Have you heard voices or sounds that other people cannot hear during these past nine months?

target_item.name: Hallucinations
target_item.manifestation: On a few of the most wired days, I could hear a low humming voice like wind over rock telling me where the dancers should move, even when I was alone in my apartment with the windows closed.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about hearing voices or sounds that others cannot hear, which directly matches hallucinations.

patient.answer:
Yes… a few times, on the most wired days. Not constantly, and not like a normal person standing there talking to me, but I did hear something.

It was this low humming voice, almost like wind moving over rock, but with words in it — or at least it felt like words. It would tell me where the dancers should move, like where a line should shift or when someone should turn or cross the space. And the strange thing was, it happened even when I was alone in my apartment, with the windows closed, so it wasn’t actually wind or people outside.

At the time I didn’t question it very much. I treated it like part of the same… message, I guess. Looking back, it scares me a little to say that, because I know other people weren’t hearing it.

Also ruled out psychotic symptoms being predominant, which would be required for schizophrenia or other psychotic disorders.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's thoughts about the mountains are currently present
doctor.question: Do you still feel like the mountains are communicating with you or have a special message for you?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: Those mountain messages and the humming voice only happened during the wired stretch when I was barely sleeping and racing through plans. Since my mood dropped, I still feel guilty and slowed down, but I haven’t heard the voice or believed the signs were directing me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the mountain-related belief is still present now, which is addressed by the profile stating those beliefs only occurred during the manic/wired period and are not present since the mood dropped.

patient.answer:
No… not now. I mean, I can still remember how real it felt, and that memory is honestly unsettling, because when I think back on it I can almost understand the logic I had at the time. But I don’t feel it happening now.

The mountain messages and that humming voice were really only during that wired stretch, when I was barely sleeping and my mind was racing through plans for the piece. Everything felt fast and connected then, like every sign or sound or bit of weather had meaning and was aimed at me. But since my mood dropped, it’s different. I feel guilty and slowed down, and kind of heavy, honestly… but I’m not hearing that voice anymore, and I’m not believing the signs are directing me.

If I see the mountains now, they’re just… mountains. Maybe they still make me emotional, because of everything that happened, but I don’t feel like they’re sending me instructions or that there’s some special message I’m supposed to decode.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of psychotic symptoms to differentiate between depressive episodes
doctor.question: Are you currently experiencing any thoughts or beliefs that seem unreal or detached from reality?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: For a while I was completely sure the mountains had singled me out to make this historic piece, and I kept taking things like trail signs, weather reports, and even strangers’ comments as instructions meant only for me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about current unreal or reality-detached beliefs, which most directly corresponds to delusions.

patient.answer:
Currently… no, I don’t think so. Not in the way it was happening before.

For a while, though, I was completely sure the mountains had singled me out for something, like I was supposed to make this historic piece and it wasn’t just my own idea. I kept treating ordinary things like they were instructions meant specifically for me — trail signs, weather reports, even strangers saying random comments that probably had nothing to do with me. At the time it all fit together so perfectly in my head that it didn’t feel questionable.

Now, when I say it out loud, I can tell that sounds detached from reality. I’m embarrassed by it, honestly. But right now I’m not actively believing that those things are messages or directions for me. It feels more like I’m looking back at something I was convinced of then, rather than something I’m convinced of today.

doctor.intent: Determine the severity of depressive symptoms
doctor.question: Do you feel like you're unable to experience pleasure in any activities most of the time?

target_item.reason: The question is about loss of pleasure or interest (anhedonia), but the provided symptom profile does not include a specific item covering anhedonia.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure I’d say unable to experience pleasure most of the time. That sounds… very total, and I don’t know if it’s quite that.

I mean, I haven’t been enjoying things in the same easy way, if that makes sense. Sometimes I’ll start something I usually like and it feels kind of muted, like I’m going through the motions and waiting for the feeling to catch up. But I can still have moments where something reaches me — a song, or a movement phrase that feels right in my body, or even just a quiet cup of coffee. It’s not completely gone.

So… no, I don’t think I’m totally unable to feel pleasure. It’s more like it’s harder to access sometimes, or it doesn’t last as long as I expect it to.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of psychomotor agitation or retardation
doctor.question: Do you feel like you're moving more slowly than usual or have trouble sitting still?

target_item.name: Psychomotor_Changes
target_item.manifestation: Recently even crossing the studio to pick up my notebook feels slowed down, like my body is moving through wet sand instead of music.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about psychomotor slowing or agitation, which directly matches psychomotor changes.

patient.answer:
Yes… more slowly, definitely. It’s strange because I’m so used to thinking of my body as something responsive, you know? Like even when I’m tired, there’s usually some kind of rhythm I can find. But lately it feels like the rhythm just isn’t there.

Even crossing the studio to pick up my notebook feels slowed down. I’ll see it across the room and think, okay, just go get it, and then my body feels like it’s moving through wet sand instead of music. That’s the best way I can describe it. Everything takes more effort than it should, and I notice myself moving in this heavy, delayed way.

I don’t feel like I’m crawling out of my skin or unable to sit still, though. It’s more the opposite — like getting myself going is the hard part.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of psychomotor agitation
doctor.question: Do you often feel restless or have an inability to sit still?

target_item.name: Psychomotor_Changes
target_item.manifestation: Recently even crossing the studio to pick up my notebook feels slowed down, like my body is moving through wet sand instead of music.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about restlessness or inability to sit still, which directly concerns psychomotor activity changes.

patient.answer:
Not really restless, no. I don’t feel like I have to keep getting up or like I can’t sit still. If anything, it’s been the opposite, and I know I already kind of said this, but it’s the part I notice most because of how physical my work is.

Recently even something simple, like crossing the studio to pick up my notebook, feels slowed down. I’ll look at it and know I need it, but getting my body to actually move feels weirdly heavy, like I’m moving through wet sand instead of music. That sounds dramatic, but that’s honestly what it feels like — not agitation, more like everything takes extra effort to start.
